text: {"score":4,"justification":"The summary is accurate and cautious, with an inconclusive lean that fits the thin documentation. Numbers match the card: 23.4% of 431 claims, expected 2.6%, score 12.69, z 3.52, 16 documented, 3 documented 99215s, 0 of 7. The 54% figure is a rounding of 54.5%. The unmatched \"99215\" is just the CPT code. The cited claims fit the sentences and are real in the card. The summary gives a concrete next step, which is to request charts for the low-complexity 99215 claims. It also flags that the records are too thin to judge. The weaknesses are a few unsupported statements and a mismatch between the prose and the code-written next_steps.","problems":["Claim that the excess 99215 share \"holds at every complexity tier\" is overstated: the 5+ tier has 0 of 1 visits at 99215, and tiers 4 and 5+ have very few visits.","Rash (C0066101) is inferred from dx R21, and abdominal pain from R10.9; these are reasonable readings of the codes but go beyond the card.","The prose next step (request charts for low-complexity 99215s) conflicts with the formal next_steps, which ask for a larger sample of 99214/99215 and a re-screen; the formal steps are generic and do not name the cited claims.","The example claims cited (C0065981, C0065983) are only 2 of the many examples used in the narrative; the cited_claim_ids omit the others named in the text, such as C0066360.","The summary states that \"most\" 99215s fall on low-complexity patients but gives 54% without the underlying counts (about 55 of 101); it also does not mention that the documented 99215 supports are only 3 claims, one without recorded minutes."]}
